messages.author: fb40a65bd21dcf6f
messages.subject: Initialise particular parameters
parts:
Hi, I have a model in which initialising a particular parameter vector helps it to find better posterior modes. However if I initialise this vector through the "init" argument to the Rstan stan() method, I think I have to initialise all the parameters. Is there anyway to avoid this? If not, could you add this as a feature? That is, if the user-supplied init function does not return a list element for a parameter then Stan would use "random" as the default.
Thanks,
John.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Initialise particular parameters
parts:
Correct, it's either all or nothing for initialization.
Allowing partial inits has been on our radar, but we've
never gotten around to it.

I added a feature request to our issue tracker:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1069

The random inits are by default [-2,2] on the constrained
scale and the transforms to constrained params are all
defined in a later chapter in the manual. It the transforms
were exposed in the interfaces, this would be easier, at
least in RStan and PyStan.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Initialise particular parameters
parts:
On Oct 7, 2014, at 2:28 PM, John Reid <johnba...@gmail.com> wrote:

...

> On a related note I was wondering if Stan is aware of the generative nature of some models. Most models I work with are described in terms of conditional distributions that have a natural order from hyperparameters through latent variables to data. I have had success initialising Stan using draws from the prior when the default "random" method didn't do so well. Are there any plans to incorporate some sort of initialisation like this? This would save users recoding their priors in init() functions (which can be error-prone).

Short answers: No and no.

This has been something Andrew's been asking for, too.
But as is, Stan has no knowledge of any generative structure
in the model, so until we add a layer on top to deal with
directed graphical models or some more restricted class, we
don't have any hooks on which to hang such an implementation.

But I'd imagine in cases where what you're suggesting would
work, Stan would also be able to just converge.

Do you have non heavily multimodal examples where initialization
makes a big difference? If so, we'd love to collect them as
test cases.

My understanding is that JAGS just initializes from the prior
means and that BUGS does what you suggest, but I could be
misremembering or confusing the two systems.

- Bob

You've hit the nail on the head, my examples have multi-modal
posteriors. I believe initialising from the prior allows the sampler to
have a much greater chance of visiting more of the modes. I'm trying to
learn a latent temporal variable that explains the data well. Each datum

smoothly vary over this pseudotime. The initialisation of the data
pseudotime parameters seems very important as Stan has trouble
reordering the data during sampling. I guess that's not the sort of
example you're looking for.

Regards,
John.

Hi John, just curious: have you found the diffuse starting points to be a problem in your models? Stan initializes all the unconstrained parameters i.i.d. uniform between -2 and 2 inclusive. When initializing from R, it should be an initialization on the constrained space. That is, if a parameter is declared as `real<lower=0,upper=1> theta;`, then it should be initialized between (0, 1).

What transformations are you doing between different parameterizations? Hopefully you're not trying to go from the constrained to the unconstrained space from R outside of Stan.

> But I'd imagine in cases where what you're suggesting would
> work, Stan would also be able to just converge.
>
> Do you have non heavily multimodal examples where initialization
> makes a big difference?  If so, we'd love to collect them as

You've hit the nail on the head, my examples have multi-modal
posteriors. I believe initialising from the prior allows the sampler to
have a much greater chance of visiting more of the modes. I'm trying to
learn a latent temporal variable that explains the data well. Each datum
has a latent pseudotime and the model's parameters are allowed to
smoothly vary over this pseudotime. The initialisation of the data
pseudotime parameters seems very important as Stan has trouble
reordering the data during sampling. I guess that's not the sort of
example you're looking for.

It is an example of what we're looking for. Without knowing the details of your model: reordering is tough, multi-modality is tough. If specific initial values are putting Stan into a single mode, that's interesting to know and perhaps one of the future generations of Stan will be able to solve the problem without a hitch (I'm thinking Riemmanian manifold HMC). Of course, if it's really multi-modal and you're not trying to do a full Bayesian inference, that opens up a lot of doors that won't get you the right expectation, but might give you something from a high posterior mode.


 

Regards,

John.

> Also if custom initialisation is so useful for

If custom initialization is really necessary, it may signal
a problem with inference in the model as Daniel pointed out.

> it would be nice to include the initialisations used with

Definitely.

>> But I'd imagine in cases where what you're suggesting would
>> work, Stan would also be able to just converge.
>>
>> Do you have non heavily multimodal examples where initialization
>> makes a big difference? If so, we'd love to collect them as
>> test cases.

> You've hit the nail on the head, my examples have multi-modal
> posteriors. I believe initialising from the prior allows the sampler to
> have a much greater chance of visiting more of the modes.

That will depend on whether unconstraining uniform(-2,2) or
the prior is more dispersed and other factors about the posterior
curvature.

In any case, you may visit more, but it's going to be impossible
to do proper Bayesian inference in highly multimodal posteriors.

We'll be adding Michael Betancourt's thermodynamic sampling (arXiv-ed),
which will probably help with a lot of these issues.

We may also may wind up doing some kind of tempered optimization,
which may be more relevant for inference under multiple modes.

> I'm trying to
> learn a latent temporal variable that explains the data well. Each datum
> has a latent pseudotime and the model's parameters are allowed to
> smoothly vary over this pseudotime. The initialisation of the data
> pseudotime parameters seems very important as Stan has trouble
> reordering the data during sampling. I guess that's not the sort of
> example you're looking for.

These are the sorts of examples we're looking for.
Unfortunately, anything with modes separated by low density
troughs is going to be pretty much impossible to mix in
practice. Like the mixture models in the manual: K-means
clustering, HMMs, and LDA. And even if you could mix, the
combinatorics will prevent proper posterior inference unless
one mode is so dominant the others can be ignored.

In this particular case, if the ordering is known, we have
a constrained parameter for ordered input.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Initialise particular parameters
parts:
On Oct 8, 2014, at 4:14 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:

> Really? I thought we’d swiched this to be uniform from -0.5 to 0.5 as default, as we were having problems with some of the more extreme starting points.

I thought so, too, but we never did.

The problems with extreme starting points went away with
better adaptation and higher acceptance rates, so we left it
at [-2,2].

It's easy to specify with init = 0.5 in RStan. The choice of 2
remains rather arbitrary. It covers a lot of logit-scaled parameters
and runs from roughly 0.1 to 10.0 on positive constrained parameters,
and we thought that looked suitably diffuse for a default.

> Also, in response to the earlier question, it would not be possible for Stan to automatically draw parameters from the prior (indeed “the prior” is not so clearly defined, as all we are specifying is a joint density function) but it would be possible to do this “manually” by doing such simulations in R and then specifying these as starting values in the Stan call.

Once we add the prior/likelihood (aka base/delta split), this
should be easy for models with proper priors.

Of course, it'll introduce all the confusion about prior/likelihood
we've been trying to avoid, but that's inevitable with the above split.

- Bob

When I say "highly multimodal", I'm talking about cases like LDA
or K-means clustering where the posterior multimodality is combinatorially
intractable (i.e., the number of modes grow exponentially and thus overwhelm any
hardware-based solution to explicitly sample from them).

If someone could solve the combinatorial intractability problem,
we have bigger fish to fry than Bayesian sampling!

>> We'll be adding Michael Betancourt's thermodynamic sampling (arXiv-ed),
>> which will probably help with a lot of these issues.

So it is. Michael even changed the title of the arXiv paper:

>> Unfortunately, anything with modes separated by low density
>> troughs is going to be pretty much impossible to mix in
>> practice.
>
> Again, just to clarify: "pretty much impossible to mix" using certain algorithms, maybe not with others.

Right. Moving between a small number of modes is not intractable in
the same way that sampling from all of them is.

- Bob
